blocks.html: Welcome to Middle Egyptian. Over two semesters you will learn to read the language of the pyramids’ successors, the stelae of Abydos, the Tale of Sinuhe and the temple walls of Karnak, sign by sign. We begin with the language itself: what kind of language it is, who its relatives are, and how long people wrote it.

Egyptian is a language of the Afroasiatic family. It forms a branch of its own, beside Semitic (Hebrew, Arabic, Akkadian), Berber, Chadic and Cushitic. It was written for more than 4,000 years, from about 3200 BC to Coptic manuscripts of the Middle Ages.

Languages are related when they descend from one ancestor. Linguists show this the way a family historian would: not by a few look-alike words, which can be borrowed, but by regular matches in grammar and basic vocabulary. Egyptian shares such features with the Semitic languages and with the Berber languages of North Africa, the Chadic languages around Lake Chad (Hausa is the best known) and the Cushitic languages of the Horn of Africa (Somali, Oromo). Together they make the Afroasiatic family.

Two features you will meet in the first weeks show the family resemblance. Feminine nouns end in -t: zꜣ “son”, zꜣt “daughter”, much as in Semitic. And the independent pronoun “I”, jnk, looks like Akkadian anāku and Hebrew ʾānōkî. Such shared grammar points back to a common ancestor far older than writing.

Why is Egyptian its own branch and not a Semitic language? Because its differences from Semitic are as deep as its likenesses: its verb system, much of its basic vocabulary and many sound correspondences go their own way. Egyptian and Semitic are cousins who split apart before either was written down.

blocks.text: More than four thousand years of writing

blocks.html: The oldest Egyptian writing goes back to about 3200 BC, near the start of Egypt’s history as one kingdom. The language changed over the following millennia, and its scripts changed with it, but it was the same language throughout. Its last stage, Coptic, was written in an alphabet from the early centuries AD. Coptic gave way to Arabic as the everyday language during the Middle Ages, and it is still used in the worship of the Coptic Church. Few languages have a written record as long.

blocks.name: eg-scripts
blocks.cap: One word through the ages: ꜥnḫ “life” in hieroglyphs and in its Coptic descendant.

blocks.html: Thinking that Ancient Egyptian is an early form of Arabic, because Egypt speaks Arabic today. Arabic is a Semitic language that came to Egypt with the Arab conquest of the 7th century AD (Alexandria fell in AD 641). It slowly replaced Coptic, the last stage of Egyptian. Egyptian and Arabic are distant cousins in the Afroasiatic family, not parent and child. Check: Coptic, the descendant of Egyptian, was still being written centuries after Arabic arrived.

blocks.title: Is it related?
blocks.q: Which of these is in the same family as Egyptian: Greek, Hausa, Persian?
steps: Greek and Persian are Indo-European languages, like English.
Hausa is a Chadic language, one of the Afroasiatic branches.

blocks.title: How long?
blocks.q: Egyptian was first written around 3200 BC, and Coptic was still copied in the AD 1300s. About how many years is that?
steps: From c. 3200 BC to AD 1: about 3,200 years (there is no year 0).
From AD 1 to AD 1300: 1,300 more years.

blocks.html: Middle Egyptian is a stage of this language, not a different language. Learning it first is like learning classical Latin before medieval Latin or Italian: it is the form most of the monuments use.

blocks.html: In What Egyptian Is you saw that Egyptian was written for more than 4,000 years. No language stays the same that long. Egyptologists divide its history into stages, each with its own grammar and spelling habits. The dates are approximate, because languages change gradually, and the written language always lagged behind the spoken one.

blocks.html: Old, Middle, Late, Demotic, Coptic: the names are stages in time. "Middle Egyptian" is the middle stage of the language, not the speech of a region.

blocks.text: Stages and scripts are different things

blocks.html: A stage is a form of the language; a script is a way of writing it. Hieroglyphs were used for monuments in every stage up to the Roman period. Hieratic, a quick, joined-up form of the signs written with a brush, was used beside them from the beginning for everyday writing. Demotic is confusingly both: the name of a stage of the language and of the very cursive script it was written in. Coptic is written in its own alphabet. So a Middle Egyptian text may be written in hieroglyphs or in hieratic; it is the same language either way.

blocks.name: eg-scripts
blocks.cap: Language stages (top) and scripts (bottom). Hieratic and Demotic are described in words: there is no accurate digital form of them.

blocks.html: Reading "Middle Egyptian" as the language of Middle Egypt, the region between the Delta and Thebes. The name refers to time: Old, Middle, Late. Egypt did have regional dialects, which show up clearly in Coptic, but the stage names are not about them. Check: Late Egyptian is not the language of "Late Egypt" either; it is simply later.

blocks.title: Which stage?
blocks.q: A tax receipt on a potsherd is written around 200 BC in the everyday language of its time. Which stage of Egyptian is it?
steps: 200 BC falls between c. 700 BC and AD 450.
That is the time of Demotic, the language (and script) of everyday documents in the Ptolemaic Period.

blocks.title: Script or stage?
blocks.q: Is "hieratic" a stage of the language?
steps: Hieratic is a way of writing, a cursive form of hieroglyphs.
It was used for Old, Middle and Late Egyptian texts alike.

blocks.html: In this course you learn Middle Egyptian. The next lesson, Why Learn Middle Egyptian, shows why it is the right place to start.

blocks.html: You now know the five stages from The Stages of Egyptian. Grammars almost always begin with the second one, Middle Egyptian. Here is why.

Middle Egyptian was the spoken language of the Middle Kingdom (c. 2055–1650 BC). It then became the classical language: scribes kept writing it on monuments, in hymns and in literature for two thousand years after it stopped being spoken, down to the temples of Roman times.

blocks.text: A language that outlived its speakers

blocks.html: By the New Kingdom, people spoke Late Egyptian. Their letters, accounts and many of their stories are in it. But when a king set up a stela, when a priest carved a hymn, or when a scribe wanted a text to sound proper and timeless, he wrote Middle Egyptian, sometimes with a few later features slipping in. The temples of the Ptolemaic and Roman periods, such as Edfu and Dendera, are still inscribed in a late form of it, with many new signs and spellings. The last dated hieroglyphic inscription, carved at Philae in AD 394, is part of the same tradition.

Middle Egyptian was also the language of the great literature: the Tale of Sinuhe, the Eloquent Peasant, the Teachings of the Middle Kingdom. New Kingdom schoolboys copied these works as classics, much as later Europeans studied Cicero and Virgil.

Why did a dead form of the language last so long? Writing on monuments was meant to last forever and to speak in the voice of tradition. The classical language carried prestige and connected a king or an official to the great past. Latin played the same role in medieval Europe, long after people spoke Italian, French or Spanish.

blocks.name: eg-scripts
blocks.cap: Middle Egyptian: spoken in the Middle Kingdom, written on monuments until the end of hieroglyphic writing.

blocks.html: Expecting every text to be in the language of its own time. A temple wall carved under the Romans is not in Demotic or Coptic: it is in (a late form of) Middle Egyptian. Check the medium: formal hieroglyphic monuments use the classical language; everyday documents of the same date use the spoken stage.

blocks.title: Why learn it first?
blocks.q: A student wants to read stelae of the Middle Kingdom, the hymns of the New Kingdom and the temple of Edfu. Which stage should she learn first?
steps: All three use Middle Egyptian (Edfu in a late form of it).
Old and Late Egyptian are then easy steps away.

blocks.title: How long after?
blocks.q: The Middle Kingdom ended about 1650 BC. The last hieroglyphic inscription is from AD 394. How long was the classical language carved after that?
steps: From c. 1650 BC to AD 1: about 1,650 years.

blocks.html: Hieroglyphs look like pictures, and it is natural to think each one means what it shows. In fact most signs in a text stand for sounds. Before you learn the signs one by one, you need the three jobs a sign can do. (You saw the language’s history in Why Learn Middle Egyptian; now we turn to the script.)

A sign can be a phonogram (it writes sounds), a logogram or word sign (it writes a whole word, by its picture), or a determinative (it is not read; it shows what kind of word it ends). Many signs can do more than one job.

items: Phonograms write one, two or three consonants: the ripple of water 𓈖 writes n, the game board 𓏠 writes mn, the heart and windpipe 𓄤 writes nfr.
Logograms write a whole word by showing it: the plan of a house 𓉐 with a stroke is pr “house”; the falcon 𓅃 is ḥr “Horus”.
Determinatives come at the end of a word and are silent: the seated man 𓀀 marks words for men, the walking legs 𓂻 words of motion, the papyrus roll 𓏛 writing and ideas.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The god Ptah: three sound signs, p t ḥ, and the seated god as determinative.

blocks.html: Why mix sound signs and picture signs? A script of pure pictures cannot write grammar (endings, pronouns, names), and a script of pure sounds would leave many words looking alike, because Egyptian writing gives no vowels. The mix gives both: sounds for precision, word signs for short common words, and determinatives to tell apart words with the same consonants.

blocks.name: eg-signsort
blocks.cap: Sort each sign by its usual job. (Some signs do other jobs in other words.)

blocks.html: Treating hieroglyphs as picture writing, so that the owl 𓅓 must mean “owl”. In a text it is almost always the sound m. Check: count the signs in a line; most of them are the two dozen one-consonant signs, which write sounds.

blocks.title: What job?
blocks.q: In rꜥ “sun, Ra”, spelled 𓂋𓂝𓇳𓏤, what is the sun disk?
steps: The mouth 𓂋 writes r and the arm 𓂝 writes ꜥ: the sounds are complete.
The sun disk adds no sound; with the stroke it shows that the word means the sun.

blocks.title: Sound or word?
blocks.q: The house sign 𓉐 with a stroke 𓏤: sound sign or word sign?
steps: The stroke marks a sign that means what it shows.

blocks.html: Now that you know the three jobs of signs from Three Kinds of Signs, the next question is practical: where does a line begin? Hieroglyphs can run in either direction, and in columns, so a reader needs a rule.
Signs of people, animals and birds face the beginning of the line. Read toward their faces. Most texts run right to left; many run left to right; columns are read top to bottom.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: Right to left: the man and woman face right, toward the start of the line.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The same word left to right: now they face left.

blocks.html: Hieroglyphs were part of art. On a doorway, the inscriptions on the two sides often mirror each other so that both face the center. Beside a figure of a king or official, the signs face the same way as the figure. Right to left was the ordinary direction, especially in hieratic, but the craftsmen chose whatever direction suited the monument.
Modern books, this course included, usually print hieroglyphs left to right, because our books run that way. Then the signs face left. When you read a real monument, first look at the faces.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: A column is read from top to bottom. Columns too can face left or right, and a block of columns is read starting from the side the signs face.

blocks.html: Why do the faces point to the start? Think of the signs as a procession walking toward the reader, or toward the figure they belong to. The first sign is at the head of the procession, so the faces look forward, toward where the reading starts.

Starting at the end the faces turn away from. If a line of birds and men faces right, start at the right edge. A quick check: the determinative (often a seated man or woman) should come at the end of a word, after its sound signs; if you meet it first, you are reading backwards.

blocks.title: Where to start?
blocks.q: In a line of signs, the quail chick and the seated man face right. Where does the line begin?
steps: They face right, so the beginning is on the right.
blocks.a: at the right: read right to left

blocks.title: A column
blocks.q: A single column of signs: which end do you start at?

blocks.html: A last practical tip: signs that have no face, like the loaf 𓏏 or the water 𓈖, give no clue by themselves. Look for the nearest person, animal, bird or snake in the line, such as the horned viper 𓆑 or the owl 𓅓, and read toward its head.

blocks.html: You know from Reading Direction which end of a line to start at. But signs are not strung out one after another like letters. Scribes arranged them in neat groups that fill imaginary squares, called quadrats. Low, wide signs are stacked; small signs sit side by side.
Read group by group from the front. Inside a group, read the top before the bottom, and the sign nearer the front before the one behind it.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The name of Ptah, numbered in reading order: the stool p on top of the loaf t (1, 2), then the wick ḥ, then the determinative.

blocks.html: In the spelling of ptḥ above, the stool 𓊪 and the bread loaf 𓏏 are both low and wide, so they share one square, stool on top. Then comes the tall wick 𓎛, alone in its square, and the seated god. Read: p, t, ḥ, then the silent determinative.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: A longer group: the opening of the offering formula, numbered in written order (you will learn its special reading order in a later unit).

items: Tall, narrow signs (the reed 𓇋, the folded cloth 𓋴, the wick 𓎛) usually stand alone or beside another narrow sign.
Low, wide signs (the mouth 𓂋, the water 𓈖, the loaf 𓏏) are stacked two or three high.
Small signs fill gaps beside or under a bigger one.

blocks.html: Why stack signs at all? A line of tall and flat signs in a row would leave ugly gaps. Egyptian craftsmen cared about the look of a text as much as its content, so they packed signs into balanced blocks. The order of reading never changes, only the arrangement.

Reading the bottom sign of a stack first, or reading a tall sign after the small signs beside it. In rn “name”, written 𓂋𓈖 with the mouth on top of the water, the reading is r then n, not n then r. Check: say the result aloud by the convention (“ren”) and see if it is a word you know.

blocks.title: Reading a stack
blocks.q: In 𓂋𓂝 (mouth above arm), which sign comes first?
steps: Top before bottom: the mouth r, then the arm ꜥ.

blocks.title: Side by side
blocks.q: In 𓊵𓏏𓊪 ḥtp “offering”, the sign 𓊵 (a loaf on a mat) sits on top, and the loaf t and the stool p sit side by side under it. In what order are the signs read?
steps: Top first: 𓊵, which writes ḥtp.
Then the bottom row, front before back: t, then p. They only repeat sounds of ḥtp.
blocks.a: top sign, then t, then p: ḥtp

blocks.html: In Three Kinds of Signs you saw that most signs write sounds. Here is the surprise: they write only consonants. Egyptian had vowels, of course, but the hieroglyphic script did not write them.

Hieroglyphs write consonants only. The vowels of Egyptian words are mostly lost. Coptic, the last stage of the language, wrote vowels, and Greek and cuneiform writings of Egyptian names give more clues.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: nfr “good”: three consonants, n f r, and no vowels.

blocks.html: The word for “good” is written with signs for n, f and r. Egyptologists say it “nefer”, but the e is a modern helper, not part of the writing. Hebrew and Arabic writing also leave out most vowels, and native readers fill them in from knowledge of the language. For Egyptian, no native speakers are left to ask.

blocks.text: Where do we learn about vowels?

items: Coptic (from about AD 200) wrote vowels with Greek letters. It shows the late form of many words: nfr became ⲛⲟⲩϥⲉ (noufe), rn “name” became ⲣⲁⲛ (ran).
Foreign writings: cuneiform letters of the Amarna age and Greek historians wrote Egyptian names and words with vowels.
Patterns in the grammar and in loanwords let scholars reconstruct some older vowels, with care and much debate.

blocks.name: eg-scripts
blocks.cap: rn “name”: consonants only in hieroglyphs; Coptic adds the vowel.

blocks.html: Why could a script get away with no vowels? In Egyptian, as in Semitic languages, the consonants carry the core meaning of a word, and vowels change with grammar. Readers who spoke the language could restore the vowels from context, so the consonants were enough.

Treating the vowels Egyptologists add as Egyptian. "Nefer", "hetep" and "netjer" are conventions for talking about words, nothing more. You will learn the convention in a later lesson. Check: the Coptic descendants of nfr and nṯr, noufe and noute, have quite different vowels.

This is why a transliteration has no vowels either. The letters ꜣ, j, ꜥ and w look like vowels to an English reader, but in Egyptian they are consonants: a glottal sound, a yod (y or a glottal stop), a sound made deep in the throat, and w. You will learn each of them in the alphabet unit.

blocks.title: Counting consonants
blocks.q: How many consonants are in ḥtp “offering”?
steps: Every letter of a transliteration is a consonant: ḥ, t, p.

blocks.title: What Coptic tells us
blocks.q: Coptic ⲣⲁⲛ (ran) comes from rn. What does it add?
steps: The consonants r and n are the same.
Coptic adds the vowel a, as the word sounded late in its history.

blocks.html: About two dozen signs write a single consonant each. Egyptologists call them the uniliteral signs, or loosely "the alphabet". They are the most common signs in any text, so they come first. You will learn them in five groups, in dictionary order. (You already know from Groups and Quadrats how signs are grouped, and from Writing Without Vowels that they write consonants only.)
The first five: the vulture 𓄿 ꜣ, the flowering reed 𓇋 j, the two reeds 𓇌 y, the forearm 𓂝 ꜥ and the quail chick 𓅱 w. All five are consonants.

blocks.html: These five are hard for English speakers because they sound like vowels to us. They are not. ꜣ was a weak consonant; scholars think it began as a kind of r or l sound and later became a glottal stop, the catch in "uh-oh", and its exact value is debated. ꜥ is a sound made by tightening the throat, still used in Arabic (ʿayn). j, the "yod", was a y sound or a glottal stop, and w was w. Egyptologists say ꜣ and ꜥ as "a", j as "i" and w as "u" when they read aloud, but that is a convention.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: ꜥnḫ “life” begins with ꜥ: the ankh sign is helped by n and ḫ, which you will meet soon.

blocks.html: Notice the yod letter: this course writes j, as Allen’s grammar does. Gardiner and other older books use a special i with a mark (ỉ or ꞽ), and some print plain i. In the answer boxes you may type j, i, ỉ or ꞽ.

Why does Egyptology need special letters like ꜣ and ꜥ at all? Because Egyptian had more consonants than the Latin alphabet has letters. Rather than borrowing awkward combinations, Egyptologists adopted a set of letters with marks, one letter for each Egyptian consonant, so every transliteration can be turned back into its sounds without doubt.

Reading ꜣ and ꜥ as the vowel a. They are two different consonants with two different signs, and words can differ only by them. Check yourself: the vulture 𓄿 is ꜣ (two little hooks, like a 3), the forearm 𓂝 is ꜥ (one hook, like a raised c).

blocks.title: Name the sound
blocks.q: Which sound does the forearm 𓂝 write?
steps: It writes the throat consonant ꜥ (typed a in MdC).

blocks.title: Two ways to write y
blocks.q: Which two signs can write y?
steps: Or two oblique strokes 𓏭, which also mark the dual.

blocks.html: The second group of one-consonant signs is easier for English speakers: these are sounds we have. Keep the first group from The Alphabet I: ꜣ j y ꜥ w in mind; the practice mixes them in.
The foot 𓃀 b, the stool 𓊪 p, the horned viper 𓆑 f, the owl 𓅓 m and the ripple of water 𓈖 n.

blocks.html: Three of these do double duty, which is why you see them everywhere. The horned viper is also the suffix pronoun =f “he, his”. The owl alone is the preposition m “in, from, as”, and the water alone is n “to, for” or “of”.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: Anubis, jnpw: the reed j, the water n, the stool p and the quail chick w, then the jackal as determinative.

items: The owl 𓅓 faces you: its head is turned to the front. Other birds you will meet (the vulture 𓄿, the quail chick 𓅱, the swallow 𓅨) are shown in profile.
The ripple of water 𓈖 is a single zigzag line. The pool 𓈙 (š, next unit but one) is a rectangle, and three ripples stacked 𓈗 mean “water” itself.
The viper 𓆑 has two little horns; the cobra 𓆓 (ḏ) has none and rears its body.

blocks.html: Why did the Egyptians choose these pictures? Many uniliterals come from words with that sound: the word for “mouth”, rꜣ, begins with r, and the mouth sign writes r. Others are less clear to us. You do not need the reasons to read; you need to know the pictures well enough to tell them apart quickly.

Confusing the owl with other birds, or the ripple of water with the pool. Look for the owl’s front-facing head, and remember that the ripple 𓈖 is a line, not a box. Check: if a word makes no sense with m, look again at the bird.

blocks.q: Read 𓇋𓈖𓊪𓅱, the first four signs of Anubis.

blocks.title: A pronoun hiding in plain sight
blocks.q: A noun is followed by 𓆑. What might it add?
steps: After a noun, f is often the suffix pronoun “his”.

blocks.html: This group is the famous one: four different h sounds. English has only one, so it takes practice. The mouth, which writes r, comes first. You already know two groups (The Alphabet I: ꜣ j y ꜥ w, The Alphabet II: b p f m n).
The mouth 𓂋 r, the reed shelter 𓉔 h, the twisted wick 𓎛 ḥ, the round sign 𓐍 ḫ and the animal’s belly 𓄡 ẖ. h, ḥ, ḫ and ẖ are four different consonants.

blocks.html: The marks matter. A dot under h, a little arc under h, a line under h: each is a different letter, and words change meaning with them. ḥr is “face” or “on”, written with the face sign; ḫr is “with, near (a person)”; and hrw is “day”.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: hrw “day”: plain h (the shelter), r (the mouth), w (the quail chick) and the sun as determinative.

blocks.cap: Sort the four h signs.

blocks.html: Why keep four letters when we pronounce two of them alike? Because the Egyptians kept them apart in spelling, so they were different sounds to them, and dictionary order depends on them: ḥ words, ḫ words and ẖ words fill separate sections. A plain h in place of ḥ is a misspelling, not a variant.

Writing a plain h for all four. ḥtp “offering” with a plain h is no word at all. When you type, use H for ḥ, x for ḫ and X for ẖ (the Manuel de Codage), or the keypad. Check: the wick 𓎛 is ḥ (dot under), the round sign 𓐍 is ḫ (arc under), the belly 𓄡 is ẖ (line under).

blocks.q: The wick 𓎛 writes which letter?
steps: The twisted wick of flax is V28.
It writes the emphatic ḥ (MdC H).

The door bolt 𓊃 z, the folded cloth 𓋴 s, the pool 𓈙 š, the hill slope 𓈎 q, the basket 𓎡 k and the jar stand 𓎼 g.

blocks.html: In Old Egyptian the door bolt and the folded cloth were two sounds, z and s. By the Middle Kingdom they had merged, and scribes used both signs for the same sound, following the traditional spelling of each word. Allen and this course write them z and s to show which sign a word uses; Gardiner and many older books write s for both (sometimes ś for the bolt). In answers, this course accepts either unless a problem says otherwise.

blocks.html: The three k-like sounds are different consonants: q (the hill slope), k (the basket) and g (the jar stand). The basket alone after a noun is often the pronoun =k “your”, said to a man.

Why keep z at all if it sounded like s? For the same reason English keeps “c” in “city”: spelling remembers history. Writing z for the bolt tells you exactly which sign stands in the word, which helps when you look a word up or copy it into hieroglyphs.

Reading the hill slope 𓈎 as k, or treating z and s as two sounds in Middle Egyptian. The hill slope is q, a separate letter; z and s were one sound by then, written two ways. Check: the hill slope has a smooth hump; the basket 𓎡 has a handle.

Why does the line matter so much? Because Egyptian has words that differ only by it. Dropping the line turns one consonant into another, just as changing “t” to “d” turns “ten” into “den”. A transliteration without the marks is a different (often meaningless) string.

Dropping the line under ṯ and ḏ. Without it, nṯr “god” would be read with a plain t, which is not the word. When you type, use T for ṯ and D for ḏ. Check the sign: the rope 𓍿 and the cobra 𓆓 always have the line; the loaf and the hand never do.

blocks.html: You now know every one-consonant sign (The Alphabet V: t ṯ d ḏ). Transliteration is the way Egyptologists write Egyptian in letters, one letter for each consonant, so that words can be printed, compared and looked up.
The Egyptological alphabet, which is also dictionary order: ꜣ j y ꜥ w b p f m n r h ḥ ḫ ẖ z s š q k g t ṯ d ḏ. Dots, hyphens and = signs inside a transliteration only show how a word is built.

Egyptian dictionaries begin with ꜣ, not with a. Then come j, y, ꜥ and w, the weak consonants, followed by the labials b p f m, then n and r, the four h sounds in the order h ḥ ḫ ẖ, the s sounds z s š, the k sounds q k g, and finally t ṯ d ḏ. Words are compared letter by letter in this order.

Capitals are used only for names in running text (Jmn, Ptḥ), never to change a letter.

blocks.html: Why a special order? It groups the sounds roughly by kind and by where they are made in the mouth. The great Berlin dictionary of Egyptian used it, and dictionaries have followed it ever since. Because every letter has one place, any word can be found without knowing how to pronounce it.

Alphabetizing transliterations in English order, putting ꜣ and ꜥ with a, or ḥ, ḫ, ẖ together with h. In an Egyptian dictionary ꜣ comes first, ꜥ comes after j and y, and h, ḥ, ḫ, ẖ are four separate sections. Check: ḏ is the last letter, so ḏd comes after dj.

blocks.html: Typing ꜣ, ḥ or ṯ is slow on most keyboards. In the 1980s Egyptologists agreed on a plain-keyboard system called the Manuel de Codage (MdC). It is used in dictionaries, databases and hieroglyph software, and you can use it in every answer box on this site. (It builds on the alphabet from Transliteration and Its Order.)
MdC typing: ꜣ A, j i, y y, ꜥ a, ḥ H, ḫ x, ẖ X, š S, ṯ T, ḏ D. Every other letter is typed as itself. Capitals carry meaning.

blocks.html: The same Manuel de Codage also writes hieroglyphs by their Gardiner codes, joined by signs that show the layout: - for the next group, : for a stack (top over bottom) and * for signs side by side. The offering formula above is M23:X1*N35-R4:X1*Q3-X8. You will not need to type codes in this course, but you will see them in sign lists.

Why letters like A and a, H and h? MdC had to fit 25 Egyptian consonants onto keys that every typewriter had. It uses lowercase for the plain letters and capitals for the marked ones that look most like them: H for ḥ, S for š, T for ṯ, D for ḏ. A and a stand for ꜣ and ꜥ, x and X for ḫ and ẖ.

Typing capitals at random, such as Ntr for nṯr. In MdC h and H are different letters (h and ḥ), and so are a and A (ꜥ and ꜣ), s and S, t and T, d and D. Capitalize only where MdC means it. Check: read your typing back letter by letter; does each capital stand for a marked letter?

blocks.html: Transliterations have no vowels (Transliteration and Its Order), but people need to say words aloud in class and in conversation. Egyptologists use a simple convention for this. It is a tool, not a reconstruction of ancient speech.
By convention: ꜣ and ꜥ are said “a”, j “i”, w “u” between consonants, and an “e” goes between other consonants. ḫ and ẖ are “kh”, š “sh”, ṯ “tj”, ḏ “dj”. So nfr is “nefer”.

blocks.html: A few famous words and names keep spellings that came into English through Greek or older scholarship: ꜥnḫ is “ankh”, jmn is “Amun”, rꜥ is “Ra” (or “Re”), ptḥ is “Ptah”, mꜣꜥt is “Maat”. Royal names are usually given in their familiar forms, such as Tutankhamun and Ramesses.

Why not try to say words as Egyptians did? Because the vowels are mostly unknown, and they changed over 3,000 years: a word of the Old Kingdom did not sound like the same word in Coptic. Any reconstruction would be uncertain and differ from scholar to scholar. A simple shared convention lets everyone understand each other.

Taking the convention for the ancient pronunciation. Nobody in ancient Egypt said “nefer”: the Coptic descendant of the word is noufe, and the Middle Egyptian vowels were different again. Check: if a book says “the Egyptians pronounced it nefer”, it is speaking loosely.

blocks.html: Compounds are said part by part: ḥtp-dj-nsw is “hetep-di-nesu”, nsw-bjt “nesu-bity”, zꜣ-rꜥ “sa-Ra”. A w after a consonant at the end of a word is “u”: nbw “gold” is “nebu”, hrw “day” is “heru”. Different teachers vary a little (some say “nesut” or “nisu”), and that is fine: the transliteration, not the sound, is what identifies the word.

Names reached English by several roads, so they come in several forms. Greek writers turned jmn-ḥtp into Amenophis, while Egyptologists say Amenhotep; the god jmn appears as Amun, Amon and Amen. When you meet two spellings of a name in two books, transliterate both: they usually turn out to be the same Egyptian word.

blocks.html: With the alphabet (The Alphabet V: t ṯ d ḏ) you can spell anything, but scribes rarely did. Most words use signs that write two consonants at once, the biliterals. There are about a hundred of them in common use; a dozen cover most texts.
A biliteral sign writes two consonants, in a fixed order: the house 𓉐 writes pr, the game board 𓏠 mn, the swallow 𓅨 wr, the basket 𓎟 nb. It writes those sounds in any word that contains them.

Such helpers are called phonetic complements, and you will study them soon. For now: a biliteral is often followed by one-consonant signs that repeat its last (or both) sounds.

blocks.html: Why are there two-consonant signs at all? They began as word signs. The house was the word pr “house”; scribes then used the same picture for the sound pr in other words, such as prj “go out”, much as a picture of a bee and a leaf can write English “belief”. That rebus principle is how most sound signs came to be.

Reading a biliteral as one sound, so that the basket 𓎟 is just “n” or just “b”. It always stands for two consonants, n and b in that order. Check: count the letters in your transliteration; each biliteral should contribute two.

blocks.html: The eye 𓁹 is a good example of how sound signs work. It writes the sound jr in jrj “to make, do”, one of the most common verbs, and in names like wsjr Osiris. Only in some spellings, with a stroke, does it mean the eye itself (jrt).

blocks.html: Why learn these sounds instead of the pictures’ meanings? Because the same picture turns up in dozens of words where its meaning has nothing to do with the word. The duck appears in “son” and “daughter” because the word for pintail duck sounded like the word for son, not because sons are ducks.

Mixing up the pintail duck and other birds, or reading the eye only as “eye”. The eye writes jr in many words, above all jrj “make”. Check: if a word has an eye sign and no stroke, read jr and see if a known word appears.

blocks.html: A smaller set of signs writes three consonants. You have met several already as words: the ankh, the sign for “good”, the offering mat. Like the biliterals of Biliteral Signs, they are sound signs as well as word signs.
Triliteral signs write three consonants: 𓋹 ꜥnḫ, 𓄤 nfr, 𓊵 ḥtp, 𓊹 nṯr, 𓆣 ḫpr, 𓋾 ḥqꜣ, 𓄊 wsr.

blocks.html: The scarab is a fine example. The dung beetle was called ḫprr, and its sign writes ḫpr in the verb “to become, come into being”. The sun god in his morning form, Khepri, and many royal names (Thutmose III’s throne name mn-ḫpr-rꜥ) use it.

Why are triliterals so often followed by extra signs? A three-consonant sign is easy to confuse with a look-alike, and a reader needs to know it is being read as sounds. So scribes added one-consonant signs that repeat the last one or two sounds, like f and r after 𓄤. These complements are the subject of the next lesson.

Reading the ankh only as the word “life”. As a sound sign it writes ꜥnḫ in other words too: ꜥnḫ “mirror” is written with it, and so are names and phrases such as Tutankhamun, twt-ꜥnḫ-jmn “living image of Amun”. Check: when the ankh appears inside a name or phrase, read the sound ꜥnḫ, then look for the meaning.

blocks.html: Many triliterals are also word signs for the word they write. The flag 𓊹 alone, or with the seated god, is nṯr “god”; the bead collar 𓋞 alone is nbw “gold”; the crook with complements and a seated man is ḥqꜣ “ruler”. Whether a sign is acting as a sound sign or as a word sign, its reading stays the same, so learn the three consonants first.

blocks.html: In Triliteral Signs you saw extra signs after a two- or three-consonant sign. These are phonetic complements: one-consonant signs that repeat sounds already written, to make the reading certain.
A phonetic complement repeats one or more consonants of a bigger sign beside it. It is not read a second time: 𓄤𓆑𓂋 is nfr, not “nfrfr”.

blocks.cap: Complements usually repeat the last one or two consonants.

items: A small one-consonant sign right after (or under) a bigger sign, repeating a sound of it, is almost always a complement.
Complements most often repeat the last consonant (mn + n) or the last two (nfr + f r, ꜥnḫ + n ḫ).
Sometimes a complement comes first and repeats the first sound, as the folded cloth s before the ear sign in sḏm “hear”.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: sḏm “hear”: the cow’s ear is the word sign, with s before it and m after it as complements.

blocks.html: Why repeat a sound? Many signs look alike, and some have more than one reading. A complement says “this sign is read with an r at the end”, which rules out other readings. It also filled out the square groups that scribes liked (see Groups and Quadrats).

Reading the complements as extra consonants, so 𓄤𓆑𓂋 becomes “nfrfr”. The f and r only confirm the reading. Check: compare the letters you have with the big sign; if a small sign repeats one of its letters, read that letter once.

Complements are a gift to the beginner. When you meet an unfamiliar big sign followed by small one-consonant signs, the small signs tell you how the big sign ends, and often that is enough to recognize the word. In a sign list, the usual complements are given with each sign for exactly this reason.

blocks.html: You now have all the pieces: one-, two- and three-consonant signs, complements (Phonetic Complements) and silent signs at the end. Here is a method for reading any word.

To read a word: (1) find where it ends, usually at a determinative; (2) read the sound signs in order, top before bottom; (3) read each consonant once, dropping complements; (4) leave out the determinative and any stroke.

blocks.html: Take 𓋾𓈎𓄿𓀀. The seated man 𓀀 at the end is a determinative: the word is about a man. The crook writes ḥqꜣ. The hill slope and the vulture repeat q and ꜣ, so they are complements. The word is ḥqꜣ, said “heqa”, “ruler”.

blocks.html: The method works on longer words too. 𓂋𓅓𓍿𓀀𓁐𓏥 has three sound signs (r, m, ṯ) and then three silent signs: a man, a woman and plural strokes. The word is rmṯ “people”, men and women together.

Why do determinatives mark the end of a word? Egyptian texts have no spaces between words. The determinative, standing at the end, works like a space and a label at once: it tells you that the word is over, and what sort of word it was.

Reading determinatives aloud as if they were sounds, so that Ptah becomes “ptḥ-nṯr” or the seated man adds an extra syllable. A word’s sounds end where its determinative begins. Check: a word ending in the seated god 𓀭 is a god’s name or the king; the sign itself adds no letters.

blocks.html: English spelling is fixed: “house” is always h-o-u-s-e. Egyptian scribes had more freedom. The same word could be written with more or fewer complements, with or without a determinative, or with a different sign. This lesson builds on Reading Whole Words.
One word can have many spellings. To decide whether two spellings are the same word, compare their transliterations, not their signs.

blocks.html: Short spellings are common in names and titles, where the word is so familiar that the reading aids are not needed; full spellings are common in careful texts. Determinatives vary too: “god” may end in the seated god 𓀭 or in the falcon on a standard 𓅆.

blocks.text: When different signs mean different words

blocks.html: The reverse also happens: two spellings can share signs and still be different words. 𓏠𓈖 is mn “remain”, but with the reed in front, 𓇋𓏠𓈖, it is jmn “Amun”. 𓉐𓏤 is pr “house”, while 𓉐𓏥 with plural strokes is prw “houses”.

Why would scribes allow so many spellings? Writing was a craft, not a standardized system enforced by dictionaries. A scribe chose a spelling to fit the space, to look balanced, or to follow the habits of his time and place. Readers coped because they read by sound and sense, as you are learning to do.

Thinking that a different spelling must be a different word. Transliterate both: 𓄤 and 𓄤𓆑𓂋 are both nfr. Check the opposite case too: a sign added at the front (the reed in jmn) changes the consonants and so the word.

blocks.html: In Three Kinds of Signs you met word signs, or logograms: signs that write a whole word by showing it. Many biliterals from Biliteral Signs began as word signs and still work as them. The question is how a reader knows when a sign means what it shows.
A sign used as a word sign is usually marked with a single stroke 𓏤 after or under it. The house with a stroke 𓉐𓏤 is pr “house”. The stroke means “this sign means what it shows”.

blocks.html: Look at zꜣ “son”. The pintail duck is not a picture of a son. The word for the duck sounded like the word for son, and the stroke still marks it as standing for the whole word. So the stroke really means “read this sign as a complete word”, even when the picture is a pun.

A low, wide sign takes the stroke underneath (𓉐𓏤, 𓇾𓏤); a tall sign takes it beside (𓅭𓏤). Feminine words put the ending first: njwt “town” is the village sign with the loaf t and the stroke side by side under it.

blocks.html: Why mark word signs at all? Because the same sign is often a sound sign elsewhere: the house writes pr in prj “go out” and is a determinative of buildings in other words. Without a marker, a reader could not tell whether to read 𓉐 as the word “house” or as two consonants in a longer word.

Reading the stroke as the number 1. Under or beside a word sign it is a marker, not a numeral. The stroke is a numeral only in numbers, where it is repeated with other number signs (see Numerals). Check: is the stroke next to a single word sign? Then it is the logogram marker.

blocks.html: In Reading Whole Words you learned to stop reading at the determinative. Now we look at what determinatives do and why Egyptian needed them.
A determinative is a silent sign at the end of a word. It shows the word’s class of meaning (a man, a woman, a god, motion, writing, a town…) and marks where the word ends. It is never read aloud.

blocks.html: Because hieroglyphs leave out vowels, many words share the same consonants. The determinative tells them apart at a glance: sn “brother” ends with a seated man, snt “sister” with a seated woman. Words of motion end with walking legs 𓂻, words for eating, speaking or feeling with a man raising his hand to his mouth 𓀁, abstract ideas with the papyrus roll 𓏛.

blocks.html: Why put the class sign at the end? Egyptian writing has no spaces. A determinative at the end works like a space with a label: the reader sees that the word has ended and what kind of thing it named. It also rescues the reader when the consonants alone are ambiguous.

Skipping determinatives entirely, or trying to pronounce them. They are silent, but they carry real information: whether the word names a man or a woman, a god, a place, an action. Check your translation against the determinative: a word ending in walking legs should be about going or coming.

blocks.html: Determinatives also help you divide a line of text into words. Faced with a long row of signs, look for the determinatives first: each one closes a word, and the signs between two of them belong to the next word. Short words without determinatives (prepositions, pronouns, particles) fill the gaps.
Some words have two determinatives, a specific one and a general one, as rmṯ “people” has a man, a woman and plural strokes. And some words, especially short common ones, have none at all.

blocks.html: About thirty determinatives cover most words in Middle Egyptian texts. Learning them is the fastest way to guess what an unknown word is about. This lesson collects the most common ones; they build on Determinatives.
The ones to know first: the seated man 𓀀, the seated woman 𓁐, the god 𓀭, the walking legs 𓂻, the man with hand to mouth 𓀁, the papyrus roll 𓏛, the house 𓉐, the town 𓊖, the hills 𓈉 and the water 𓈗.

blocks.html: The three hills 𓈉 mark foreign lands and the desert, which Egyptians grouped together: hilly country outside the flat valley. The mountain 𓈋, with two peaks and a valley between, is a different sign, the biliteral ḏw “mountain”. And the papyrus roll 𓏛 is never a sound sign: it marks words for writing (a book, a document) and for abstract ideas such as mꜣꜥt “truth”.

Why does an idea like “truth” take a papyrus roll? Because the roll stood for writing and knowledge in general, and from there for anything that cannot be pictured. The choice of determinatives shows how Egyptians grouped the world: buildings with the house, liquids with water, emotions with the mouth.

Confusing the papyrus roll with a sound sign, or the three hills (foreign land) with the mountain sign ḏw. Neither the roll nor the hills is read; the mountain is read ḏw. Check: if a word ends in three hills, think of a foreign land or the desert.

blocks.html: Scribes showed respect in their writing. When a phrase contained a word for a god or the king, that word was moved to the front, even if it belonged later in the phrase. Egyptologists call this honorific transposition. You need Logograms and the Stroke to follow the examples.

A word for a god or the king is written first out of honor but read in its normal place. The offering formula is written “king – offering – give” but read ḥtp-dj-nsw “an offering that the king gives”.

blocks.html: Sometimes the god’s name comes first because it really belongs first. jmn-ḥtp Amenhotep means “Amun is content”: Amun is the subject, so it is read first. rꜥ-ms-sw Ramesses and ḏḥwtj-ms Thutmose also begin with the god in reading. The rule is about where the word belongs grammatically, so you sometimes need the meaning to know the reading.

Why move the honored word? Putting the god or king first gave them the place of honor at the head of the phrase, visually above or before everything else. Reading, however, follows the grammar of speech, and speech did not change. The writing is polite; the language is ordinary.

Reading the signs in written order: “nsw ḥtp dj” or “jmn twt ꜥnḫ”. The honored word moves forward in writing only. Check: translate both ways; only the transposed reading gives good Egyptian grammar (“an offering that the king gives”, not “king offering gives”).

blocks.html: Egyptian nouns have a plural ending (you will learn its forms in the nouns unit), but the script often shows “more than one” in other ways too. This lesson is about the writing; it builds on Logograms and the Stroke.
The plural is shown in writing by three strokes 𓏥, by writing a sign three times, or by spelling out the ending -w. Three means “many”: it is not the number 3.

blocks.html: The ending -w is often left out of the writing even when the word is plural; the strokes or the tripled sign do the work, and the transliteration supplies it: prw, nṯrw. Some words, like rmṯ “people”, take plural strokes because they name a group, even though they are grammatically singular.

Feminine plurals are written the same ways. The plural strokes may follow the ending t and the determinative, and the transliteration then writes the full ending -wt, as you will see in The Plural. Whatever the writing, the reading rule is simple: if you see three strokes or a tripled sign, translate a plural.
Two strokes 𓏭 or a sign written twice can show the dual, the form for pairs, which you will meet in The Dual.

Why three? In Egyptian thinking, one is one, two is a pair, and three is the first “many”. Writing a sign three times is the oldest way of saying “several of these”; the three strokes are a short form of the same idea.

Reading the plural strokes as a number 3 or as a sound. They say only “more than one”. Numbers use the single stroke repeated in a group with other numerals, and 𓏥 never adds a consonant. Check: a word with plural strokes should be translated as a plural, whatever the number of things.

blocks.html: With reading under way, we turn to grammar. Every Egyptian noun is either masculine or feminine. You can usually tell which from the ending, and you will need to, because adjectives, pronouns and the word for “of” all agree with the noun. Word signs from Logograms and the Stroke appear in the examples.

Feminine nouns end in -t, written with the bread loaf 𓏏: zꜣ “son”, zꜣt “daughter”. Masculine nouns have no ending. Things have gender too: pr “house” is masculine, pt “sky” and njwt “town” are feminine.

blocks.html: Gender in grammar is a class, not always a matter of sex. A house (pr), a land (tꜣ) and a heart (jb) are masculine; the sky (pt), a town (njwt), a foreign land (ḫꜣst) and truth (mꜣꜥt) are feminine. Abstract ideas are very often feminine. When you learn a noun, learn its gender with it; the ending is your best guide.

The feminine t was weak in speech. By the time of Coptic it had usually disappeared from the end of words: snt “sister” became ⲥⲱⲛⲉ (sōne). In Middle Egyptian writing, though, it is regularly written, so it is a dependable sign of a feminine noun.

Why does gender matter so much? Because Egyptian grammar keeps track of it everywhere. An adjective after a feminine noun takes -t (zꜣt nfrt “a good daughter”), the word for “of” changes (nt), and “this” has a feminine form (tn). Getting the gender right is the first step to getting the whole phrase right.

Thinking that every final t is feminine. Some masculine words end in t as part of the root: jt “father” is masculine (its older form was jtf, and the f is often still written). Check the meaning and, when in doubt, a dictionary, which lists the gender of each noun.

Masculine plural: -w. Feminine plural: -wt, with the w before the t. nṯr “god”, nṯrw “gods”; nṯrt “goddess”, nṯrwt “goddesses”.

blocks.html: The rulers the Egyptians called ḥqꜣw ḫꜣswt “rulers of foreign lands” gave us the word “Hyksos”, through Greek. Both nouns are plural: ḥqꜣw (masculine, -w) and ḫꜣswt (feminine, -wt). It is a direct genitive, which you will meet in The Direct Genitive.

Why does the feminine plural put w before t? Because the plural marker w comes right after the stem, and the feminine t closes the word in both numbers: nṯr-t, nṯr-w-t. Think of it as stem + plural + feminine.
Writing the feminine plural as -tw (“nṯrtw”). The ending is -wt: nṯrwt. Check: take off the feminine t, add w, and put the t back at the end.

Watch for nouns that already end in w. The plural ending is added all the same: hrw “day” becomes hrww “days”, ḏw “mountain” becomes ḏww. And some nouns name a group, such as rmṯ “people”: they take plural strokes in writing although they are not built with the ending -w. When the writing leaves the number unclear, an adjective or pronoun that agrees with the noun often shows which number the scribe meant, because it takes the plural ending too.

blocks.html: English has two numbers, one and many. Egyptian has three: singular, plural (from The Plural) and the dual, for two of something, especially natural pairs.
The dual ends in -wj for masculine nouns and -tj for feminine ones: nṯrwj “the two gods”, ꜥwj “the two arms”, sntj “the two sisters”, jrtj “the two eyes”.

blocks.html: Two duals appear on almost every royal monument. tꜣwj “the Two Lands” is Egypt itself, Upper and Lower Egypt together: the king is nb tꜣwj “lord of the Two Lands”. nbtj “the Two Ladies” are the goddesses Nekhbet and Wadjet, vulture and cobra, who protect the king; one of his five names is named after them.

blocks.html: The script shows the dual by writing a sign twice, or by two oblique strokes 𓏭 after it, much as three strokes show the plural. The ending may also be spelled out with the quail chick and two reeds or strokes. Whatever the spelling, the transliteration writes -wj or -tj.

Why keep a dual at all? Many languages once had one (Old English, Greek and Arabic still show traces). It is natural for things that come in pairs: eyes, hands, feet, arms, and for pairs like the Two Lands or the Two Ladies. Egyptian kept it alive through the Middle Kingdom, though later it faded.

Using the plural for pairs of things like hands and eyes. Two hands are drtj, not drwt. Check: if the text means exactly two, and especially a natural pair, expect the dual; the plural is for three or more, or for an unspecified number.

The Two Lands were a favorite theme of royal art. A motif called smꜣ-tꜣwj “uniting the Two Lands” shows two figures tying the plants of Upper and Lower Egypt together, often carved on the sides of royal thrones. The dual in the king’s title nb tꜣwj carries the same idea: one ruler over a land made of two halves.

The direct genitive: noun A followed directly by noun B means “A of B”. The thing possessed comes first: pr nsw “the house of the king”, nb tꜣwj “the lord of the Two Lands”.

blocks.html: The two nouns form a tight unit. Usually nothing comes between them, and an adjective describing the first noun goes after the whole pair. The direct genitive is common in titles and fixed expressions; for looser connections Egyptian often uses the indirect genitive, the next lesson.

Why does the possessed noun come first? Egyptian puts the head of a phrase first and the words that describe it after: noun then adjective (zꜣ nfr “a good son”), noun then possessor (zꜣ nsw “the king’s son”). English “the house of the king” has the same order; only English “the king’s house” reverses it.
Reversing the order, reading “king’s house” as nsw pr. That would mean “the king of the house”. Check: translate the first noun first and put “of the” before the second.

Many direct genitives became fixed titles and names. zꜣ nsw “king’s son” was a rank at court; ḥmt nsw “king’s wife” is the usual title of a queen; pr-ꜥꜣ “the Great House”, the palace, came to mean the king himself, and through Hebrew and Greek it gave us the word “pharaoh”. Watch the first noun: when it is nb “lord” or nbt “lady”, the phrase means “lord of…” or “lady of…”, as in nbt pr “lady of the house”.

blocks.html: The second way to say “of” uses a little word between the nouns: the genitival adjective n. It builds on The Direct Genitive and on the plural endings of The Plural.
The indirect genitive: A + n + B. The n agrees with the first noun: n after a masculine singular, nt after a feminine singular, nw after a plural.

blocks.html: In hieroglyphs n is the water sign 𓈖, nt adds the loaf 𓏏, and nw is often the pot 𓏌 (which writes nw) or the water with a w. The word behaves like an adjective of the first noun, which is why it agrees with it: literally “the son, the one of the ruler”.

Both mean “of”. The direct genitive is usual for close, fixed pairs (titles, set phrases). The indirect genitive is used for looser relations, when an adjective or other word must come between, and very often in ordinary prose. You will read pr nsw and pr n nsw both, with the same meaning.

blocks.html: Why does the genitive word agree with the first noun and not the second? Because it describes the first noun: it is an adjective meaning “belonging to”, and adjectives agree with the noun they describe. The second noun is just its complement.
Making the genitive agree with the second noun. In pr n njwt “the house of the town”, the n is masculine because pr is masculine, even though njwt is feminine. Check: look back, not ahead.

The genitival adjective is also how Egyptian builds many descriptive phrases. ḥqꜣ n kmt is “the ruler of Egypt” (kmt, “the Black Land”, Egypt’s own name for itself); jmj-rꜣ pr n nsw could describe a steward of the king. When you translate, “of” is nearly always right; sometimes English prefers an adjective or a possessive instead.

blocks.html: Adjectives describe nouns: a good son, a great god. In Egyptian they behave in two ways that English adjectives do not. They come after the noun, and they change their ending to match it. Both ideas build on Masculine and Feminine, The Plural and the word order you saw in The Indirect Genitive.
An adjective follows its noun and agrees with it in gender and number: z nfr “a good man”, zꜣt nfrt “a good daughter”, nṯrw nfrw “good gods”.

blocks.html: The endings are the ones you already know from nouns: nothing for masculine singular, -t for feminine, -w for masculine plural, -wt for feminine plural. In hieroglyphs the plural ending of an adjective is often not written out, and a feminine plural adjective may be spelled like the singular; the transliteration and your translation follow the noun.

blocks.html: An adjective can also stand alone as a noun: nfr “a good one, something good”, wrw “the great ones, the nobles”, nfrt “good things” (the feminine is often used for “a thing”). Context decides. In ḫt nbt nfrt “every good thing” from the offering formula, both nbt and nfrt agree with the feminine noun ḫt “thing”.

Why agreement? It ties the adjective to its noun when words pile up. In a long phrase like “the good daughters of the great king”, the endings show which adjective goes with which noun, even if the order shifts. Agreement is the glue of Egyptian noun phrases.

Putting the adjective first, as in English. nfr zꜣt does not mean “a good daughter”; with the adjective first it is a sentence, “the daughter is good” (see The Adjectival Sentence). Check: in a noun phrase, the noun comes first and the adjective carries the noun’s ending.

blocks.html: Egyptian has a handy way of making adjectives from nouns and prepositions: add the ending -j. The result is called a nisbe (an Arabic grammatical term, from the same kind of adjective in Arabic). You need Adjectives, because nisbes agree just like other adjectives.
A nisbe adds -j to a noun or a preposition and means “belonging to, having to do with”: njwt “town” → njwtj “of the town, a townsman”; ḥr “on” → ḥrj “who is on, upper”.

blocks.html: Note jmj: the preposition m becomes jm when anything is attached to it, so its nisbe is jmj “who is in”. You will meet the same change in Prepositions with Pronouns.

Nisbes agree like other adjectives: feminine -jt (often written simply -t), masculine plural -jw. Many famous titles and epithets are nisbes. ẖrj-ḥbt “the one who carries the ritual book” is a lector priest; jmj-rꜣ, built from jmj “who is in” and rꜣ “mouth”, is an overseer; and Osiris is ḫntj-jmntjw “Foremost of the Westerners”, the westerners being the dead, who were buried on the west bank.

blocks.html: Why is the nisbe so useful? Egyptian has few basic adjectives, and the nisbe lets the language make new ones from any noun or preposition: “of the town”, “of the West”, “who is under”. A preposition with -j becomes an adjective “who is (in that position)”, which is how so many titles were built.
Reading a nisbe as a plain noun. nṯrj is not “god” but “divine”; ḥrj is not “face” but “who is on, upper”. Check for the -j ending and translate “belonging to…” or “who is…”.

blocks.html: One adjective is so common that it gets its own lesson: nb “every, all”. It is written with the same basket as nb “lord”, so you need its position to tell them apart. It agrees like the adjectives of Adjectives.
nb after a noun means “every, all” and agrees with it: tꜣ nb “every land”, ḫt nbt “everything”, nṯrw nbw “all the gods”. Before a noun, nb is the noun “lord”: nb tꜣwj “lord of the Two Lands”.

blocks.cap: The basket nb: “lord” before a noun, “every” after one.

blocks.html: The basket 𓎟 writes both words. Position decides. If nb comes first and a noun follows, it is the noun “lord” in a direct genitive: nb pt “the lord of the sky”. If it follows a noun, it is the adjective “every”: pt nb would be “every sky”. The same goes for the feminine: nbt pr “the lady of the house”, but pr nb “every house”.
You will meet nb “every” constantly in the offering formula: ḫt nbt nfrt wꜥbt “every good and pure thing”. The noun ḫt is feminine, so all three adjectives take -t.

Why does one sign serve both words? Both are written nb, and Egyptian writing spells sounds, not meanings. The two words were probably distinct in speech (their vowels may have differed), but the script cannot show it. Word order, which is strict in Egyptian, does the work instead.
Confusing nb “every” with nb “lord”. After a noun it is “every”; before a noun it is “lord of”. Check the order: tꜣ nb “every land”, nb tꜣ “the lord of the land”.

When nb follows a noun that already has an adjective, it usually comes right after the noun: ḫt nbt nfrt “every good thing”. And with a suffix pronoun, as in ḫt=f nbt “all his things, all his property”, it follows the suffix. In every case it keeps the gender and number of its noun.

blocks.html: Demonstratives point: “this man”, “that town”, “these gods”. Middle Egyptian has a small set, and like adjectives (Adjectives) most of them follow the noun and agree with it. One group goes in front, and it has a future: it became the Late Egyptian word for “the”.
pn (masculine) and tn (feminine) “this” and pf, tf “that” follow the noun: z pn “this man”, njwt tn “this town”. pꜣ, tꜣ, nꜣ “this, these” and nn “these” come before it.

blocks.html: The p-forms are masculine and the t-forms feminine, the same contrast as the feminine ending -t. zꜣ pn “this son”, zꜣt tn “this daughter”; nṯr pf “that god”, ḫꜣst tf “that foreign land”.

blocks.text: The plural, and the ones that go first

blocks.html: For “these”, Middle Egyptian usually puts nn before the noun and joins them with the genitive n: nn n zꜣw “these sons”, literally “these of sons”. In the same way pꜣ, tꜣ and nꜣ n stand before the noun: pꜣ z “this man”, tꜣ ḥmt “this woman”. These front forms belong to livelier, more everyday language; in Late Egyptian they lost their pointing force and became the definite article: pꜣ “the”.

blocks.html: Why two sets? pn and tn behave like adjectives, and Egyptian adjectives follow their nouns. pꜣ, tꜣ and nꜣ behave differently: they stand at the head of the phrase, the place an English article takes, which is one reason they could develop into the article of Late Egyptian.
Putting pn before the noun. pn and tn follow their noun; only pꜣ, tꜣ, nꜣ and nn go first. Check: “this man” is z pn or pꜣ z, never “pn z”.

When a noun has both an adjective and a demonstrative, the demonstrative usually comes first, right after the noun: z pn nfr “this good man”. And pn and tn can stand alone as pronouns, “this one”. The little word pw, which you will meet in Sentences with pw, is another old demonstrative that came to be used to make sentences.

blocks.html: Egyptian has three sets of personal pronouns. The most frequent are the suffix pronouns, little endings attached to the end of a word. You already know two of their signs from the alphabet: the horned viper 𓆑 and the basket 𓎡. Gender matters here, as in Masculine and Feminine.
The suffix pronouns: =j I, my; =k you, your (to a man); =ṯ you, your (to a woman); =f he, his; =s she, her; =n we, our; =ṯn you, your (plural); =sn they, their.

blocks.html: The first person is special. Its suffix =j is usually written with a picture of the speaker: a seated man 𓀀 if a man speaks, a seated woman 𓁐 if a woman does, and a seated god if a god does. Often it is not written at all, and the reader supplies it from context. The = sign in transliteration simply shows where the suffix joins the word.

blocks.text: Gender in the second and third persons

blocks.html: Egyptian distinguishes “you” said to a man (=k) from “you” said to a woman (=ṯ), and of course “he” (=f) from “she” (=s). In the plural there is no gender difference: =ṯn for any group addressed, =sn for any group spoken of.

blocks.html: Why attach pronouns to words? Short, unstressed pronouns tend to lean on the word before them in many languages; in Egyptian they fused into suffixes. That is why they are tiny (one or two consonants) and why they can never stand alone or at the start of a sentence.
Writing =f for “she”. =f (the viper) is “he, his”; =s (the folded cloth) is “she, her”. Check: f for the fellow, s for she.

blocks.html: You know the forms from Suffix Pronouns. Now look at what they do. The same suffix means different things depending on the word it is attached to.

On a noun, a suffix pronoun is possessive: pr=f “his house”. On a preposition, it is the object: n=f “to him”, ḥnꜥ=j “with me”. (On a verb, it is the subject; you will meet that in Middle Egyptian II.)

blocks.cap: ḥm=f “His Majesty”, literally “his majesty”: the noun ḥm with the suffix =f. Egyptian texts refer to the king this way constantly.

blocks.html: With a noun, the suffix always comes right after the noun, before any adjective: zꜣ=f nfr is “his good son” (more literally, “his son, the good one”). With a feminine noun, the t stays: njwt=f “his town”, zꜣt=s “her daughter”.

blocks.text: A phrase you will read often

blocks.html: ḥm=f “His Majesty” is a noun with a suffix. The noun ḥm, translated “majesty”, is used with every pronoun: ḥm=k “Your Majesty”, ḥm=s “Her Majesty” (of a queen like Hatshepsut). Stories and annals say jw ḥm=f m ... “His Majesty was in ...” to set the scene.

Why can one pronoun be both “his” and “him”? Because the suffix simply marks a person attached to a word; the word decides the relation. English does something similar with “of him” and “his”. Egyptian just uses one short form for all of it.
Putting the suffix before the noun, as with English “his house”. It always comes after: pr=f, never “f pr”. Check: the noun or preposition first, the person last.

The suffix is also how Egyptian says “mine, yours” and builds many set phrases. nb=j “my lord” is the polite way to address a superior; bꜣk=k “your servant” is the humble way to refer to oneself in a letter, much as English letters once said “your humble servant”. When you see a suffix on a title or a kinship word, translate it with the matching possessive and think about who is speaking to whom.

blocks.html: The second set of pronouns is the dependent pronouns. They are separate little words, not suffixes, but they cannot begin a sentence: they always follow (depend on) another word. You need Suffix Pronouns to compare them.
The dependent pronouns: wj me, ṯw you (man), ṯn you (woman), sw him, sj her, st it, them, n us, ṯn you (plural), sn them.

blocks.html: In the plural the dependent pronouns look like the suffixes (n, ṯn, sn), so their position tells them apart: a suffix is attached with = to the word before it; a dependent pronoun stands as a word of its own. In the singular the forms differ clearly: sw and sj against =f and =s.

Why have a second set at all? The suffix pronouns are bound to the word they follow and mean “my, his…” on nouns. The dependent pronouns can stand as a separate word in the sentence, which is what an object or the subject after a particle needs. Each set fills its own positions.

Using a suffix pronoun as the object of a verb, or after mk. “Look, she is in the house” is mk sj m pr, with the dependent sj, not mk=s. Check: if the pronoun is a separate word after mk, a verb or an adjective, it is dependent.

blocks.html: The third set, the independent pronouns, can stand on their own, and they usually stand first. They complete the picture begun in Suffix Pronouns and Dependent Pronouns.
The independent pronouns: jnk I, ntk you (man), ntṯ you (woman), ntf he, nts she, jnn we, ntṯn you (plural), ntsn they. They head a sentence: jnk zꜣ=k “I am your son”.

blocks.cap: The independent pronouns: most are nt + a suffix pronoun.

blocks.html: Most of the forms are easy to remember: nt plus the suffix pronoun. ntf is nt + f, nts is nt + s. Only the first person differs: jnk “I” and jnn “we”.

blocks.cap: jnk “I”: reed j, water n, basket k.

blocks.html: An independent pronoun usually stands at the head of a sentence, as the subject of a noun predicate: jnk sš “I am a scribe”, ntk nb=j “you are my lord”, ntf jt=j “he is my father”. It often carries emphasis: “I am the one who…”. You will build such sentences in The Nominal Sentence.

Why does Egyptian need a stressed pronoun? The suffix and dependent pronouns are unstressed and cannot start a sentence. When the speaker wants to put the person first, as the subject of “I am X” or for emphasis, a full, stressed word is needed. That is the independent pronoun.

Using jnk where English says “me”, as an object: “he saw me” is not “he saw jnk” (the object would be wj). jnk is used like “I am the one”, at the head of a sentence. Check: does the pronoun begin the sentence as its subject? Then an independent pronoun fits.

Independent pronouns also carry the claims of tomb autobiographies, where the owner speaks about his own good conduct. Many of his sentences begin with jnk: “I was one who gave bread to the hungry…”, “I was one beloved of his lord…”. You will read such texts in Middle Egyptian II. In each case the pronoun comes first and carries weight, which is the key to all its uses.

blocks.html: Prepositions are the small words that say where, when, to whom and how: “in the house”, “to the god”, “like Ra”. Several of them are single signs you know from the alphabet (The Alphabet V: t ṯ d ḏ). They are among the most frequent words in any text.
The simple prepositions: m “in, from, as”, n “to, for”, r “to, toward”, ḥr “on, upon”, ḫr “with, near (a person)”, ḥnꜥ “together with”, jn “by”, mj “like”. The preposition comes before its noun.

Example

blocks.html: m is the busiest. With a place it means “in” or “at” (m njwt “in the town”). After a verb of going out it means “from” (prj m pr “go out from the house”). Before a noun of role or kind it means “as, being”: jw=f m sš “he is a scribe”, literally “he is as a scribe”. Gardiner calls this the m of predication. The other prepositions also have a range of senses, which a dictionary lists with examples.
r has a useful special use: after an adjective it means “than”. wr r is “greater than”, so a text can say a king is wr r nṯrw “greater than the gods”.

Why are such short words so flexible? Prepositions in every language stretch from a basic sense (place) to related ones (time, cause, manner). English “in” covers “in the house”, “in an hour” and “in anger”. Egyptian m stretches further, covering both “in” and “from”, because the context of the verb makes the direction clear.

Giving m only one meaning. Its sense depends on context: “in”, “from”, “as”, even “with” (of an instrument). Check: translate with “in” first; if the sentence speaks of leaving or coming out, try “from”; if the noun names a role, try “as”.

blocks.html: Prepositions take objects, and when the object is a pronoun it is a suffix pronoun (Suffix Pronouns). The pattern is the same as with nouns: the suffix goes on the end. One preposition changes its shape.
Preposition + suffix pronoun: n=f “to him”, ḥr=s “on it, on her”, ḥnꜥ=j “with me”. Before a suffix, m becomes jm: jm=f “in it, in him”.

blocks.html: There is no separate word for “it” as the object of a preposition: Egyptian uses the masculine or feminine suffix, depending on the gender of the thing. jm=f can mean “in it” when “it” is a masculine noun like a house, and jm=s when it is a feminine noun like a town.

A word of one consonant, m, cannot carry a suffix comfortably, so it takes a helping j: jm=f, jm=sn. The same longer form appears in the nisbe jmj “who is in” (Nisbe Adjectives) and in the adverb jm “there, therein”, which stands at the end of a clause.

Why a suffix and not a dependent pronoun after a preposition? Because a preposition with its object behaves like a noun with its possessor: both are a word with a person attached. Egyptian uses the same attached pronoun for both, as you saw in Using Suffix Pronouns.
Writing m=f. Before a suffix, m becomes jm: jm=f. Check: whenever the owl preposition takes a pronoun, look for the reed in front of it.

Prepositions with suffixes are everywhere in letters and speeches: n=k “to you, for you” in greetings, ḥnꜥ=sn “with them” in accounts of expeditions, r=f “against him” in descriptions of battle. Read the preposition first, then ask who the suffix refers to: the nearest suitable noun of the same gender and number is usually the answer.

blocks.html: Egyptian makes many more prepositions by joining a simple preposition (The Simple Prepositions) to a noun, usually a part of the body or a word for a place. English does the same with “in front of” or “on top of”.
Compound prepositions are a simple preposition + a noun, used as one word: m-bꜣḥ “in the presence of”, m-ḫt “after”, ḥr-ḥꜣt “before, in front of”, r-gs “beside”. Learn them as wholes.

blocks.html: The literal meaning does not always predict the English one. m-ḫt means both “after” in time and “behind” in place. m-ꜥ contains ꜥ “arm, hand” and means “from (a person)” when you receive something from someone. Your dictionary lists each compound under its noun, with the senses it has.

Why build prepositions from body parts? Because the body is the easiest map of space: the face is in front, the back is behind, the hand is where things are held. Many languages, including English (“in front of”, “at the foot of”, “at the head of”), grow new prepositions this way.

Translating each part separately, so that ḥr-ḥꜣt becomes “on the front” and m-ꜥ “in the arm”. Learn compound prepositions as wholes. Check: if a word-for-word rendering sounds odd, look for the compound in the dictionary.

Compound prepositions are especially common in formal texts. An official tells how he stood m-bꜣḥ the king, in the king’s presence; offerings are laid ḥr-ḥꜣt a god, in front of him; and a son acts m-ḫt his father, after him. Each time, translate the compound as one unit and then add its object.

blocks.html: You can now build noun phrases and prepositional phrases. Put them together and you have your first Egyptian sentences, with no verb at all. Egyptian has three kinds of sentences without verbs; the first, and the most common, says where or how something is. It uses the prepositions of The Simple Prepositions and the adjectives and nouns of Adjectives.
The adverbial sentence: subject + a prepositional phrase or adverb. z m pr “the man is in the house”. Egyptian needs no word for “is”: the subject and “where” make a whole sentence.

blocks.html: The predicate (what is said about the subject) is adverbial: a preposition with its noun, or an adverb such as jm “there”. Its tense comes from context. ḥm=f m njwt can be “His Majesty is in the town” or, in a story set in the past, “His Majesty was in the town”.

blocks.html: In this bare form the sentence is common in clauses that continue a story or describe circumstances. At the start of an independent statement, Middle Egyptian usually puts a word in front of it, most often jw or mk. That is the next lesson, jw and mk. The structure of the sentence stays the same.

Why no verb “to be”? Many languages, among them Arabic, Hebrew and Russian, say “the man in the house” for “the man is in the house” in the present. The connection between subject and place is clear without a verb. Egyptian does have a verb wnn “to be, exist”, but it is used when the grammar needs a verb form, for example after certain words or to mark the future.

Looking for a verb “is” and, not finding one, reading the sentence as a phrase like “the man of the house”. If a prepositional phrase follows the subject, it is a sentence: subject + where. Check: a direct genitive has two nouns side by side; an adverbial sentence has a preposition between them.

blocks.html: Most adverbial sentences (The Adverbial Sentence) in Middle Egyptian texts begin with a small introductory word. The two you will meet constantly are jw and mk. They take pronouns differently, which is where the pronoun sets of Dependent Pronouns pay off.

jw introduces a statement and takes a suffix pronoun: jw=f m pr “he is in the house”. mk “look!” takes a dependent pronoun: mk wj m pr “look, I am in the house”. Both can also take a noun: jw z m pr, mk z m pr.

blocks.html: jw has no English equivalent. It marks the sentence as a statement in its own right, often of a fact or a situation that matters to what follows. Grammarians still discuss its exact force, but for translation the rule is simple: usually leave it out. jw=f m pr is “he is in the house” (or “he was in the house”).

mk, on the other hand, is a real word: “look!, see!”, used to draw a listener’s attention. It agrees with the person addressed: mk to a man, mṯ to a woman, mṯn to several people. In translation “look,” or “see,” is fine, or sometimes “now,” at the start of a speech.

Why do jw and mk take different pronouns? mk already contains a suffix: the k is the =k of the person addressed (“look, you”), which is why it changes to mṯ for a woman and mṯn for several people. Since its suffix slot is taken, the subject after it must be a separate word, a dependent pronoun. jw has a free slot, so a suffix pronoun attaches to it, as to nouns and prepositions.
Translating jw as a word like “and” or “then”. It has no simple English equivalent; usually leave it out. And do not put a suffix after mk or a dependent pronoun after jw: jw=s but mk sj.

blocks.html: The second kind of sentence without a verb says what or who someone is: “I am your son”, “you are my lord”. It uses the independent pronouns of Independent Pronouns.
In a nominal sentence the predicate is a noun. The commonest pattern puts an independent pronoun first: jnk zꜣ=k “I am your son”, ntk nb=j “you are my lord”, ntf jt=j “he is my father”.

Meaning
blocks.cap: Independent pronoun + noun: “I am…, you are…”.

blocks.html: The pronoun often carries emphasis: jnk zꜣ=k can be “I am your son” or “it is I who am your son”, depending on the context. Such sentences are common in speeches, in letters and in the self-presentations of tomb owners.

Egyptian can also make a nominal sentence of two nouns with nothing between them, “A is B”, but in Middle Egyptian this bare pattern is rare and limited to certain expressions. Most sentences of the type “A is B” use either an independent pronoun (this lesson) or the little word pw, which is the next lesson, Sentences with pw.

Why an independent pronoun here? The subject of a nominal sentence stands first and is stressed, and only the independent pronouns can stand first on their own. A suffix pronoun cannot begin a sentence, and a dependent pronoun must follow another word, so neither can do this job.

Confusing a nominal sentence with the direct genitive. pr nsw is a noun phrase, “the house of the king”; jnk zꜣ=k is a sentence because it starts with an independent pronoun. Check: does the group begin with jnk, ntk, ntf, nts…? Then it is a sentence “X is…”.

Notice that the noun after the pronoun can be anything a noun phrase can be: a bare noun (sš “a scribe”), a noun with a suffix (zꜣ=k “your son”), a direct genitive (jnk zꜣ nsw “I am a king’s son”), or a noun with an adjective (jnk sš nfr “I am a good scribe”). The pronoun stays first, and the whole rest of the sentence is its predicate. Egyptian has no articles, so “a scribe” and “the scribe” look the same: choose whichever suits the context.

blocks.html: The little word pw was once a demonstrative, “this” (compare This and That). In Middle Egyptian it is mainly used to make sentences of the type “it is X” or “A is B”. It completes the nominal sentences of The Nominal Sentence.
pw placed after a noun or noun phrase makes a sentence “it is (that)”: zꜣ=j pw “it is my son” (or “he is my son”), nṯr pw “it is a god”.

blocks.html: pw follows the whole first noun phrase, however long: pr nsw pw “it is the house of the king”, with pw after the direct genitive, not inside it. English translates pw with “it is”, “he is”, “she is” or “this is”, as the context requires: pw itself does not change for gender or number.

There is also a longer pattern, A pw B, used in definitions and explanations, with pw standing between the two parts. You will meet it in reading texts; the short pattern of this lesson is the place to start.

Why does a word for “this” make a sentence? Pointing words often turn into linking words. Saying “my son, this” is very close to saying “this is my son”. Over time pw lost its pointing force and became a sentence marker, a little like a copula.

Putting pw at the start of the sentence. It comes after the first noun or noun phrase: zꜣ=j pw, never “pw zꜣ=j”. And do not confuse it with pn “this”: zꜣ=j pw is a sentence, zꜣ pn a phrase “this son”.

Sentences with pw are common in explanations and answers. A text may ask a question and answer with a pw-sentence: “who is he? jt=j pw”, “he is my father”. Religious texts use them to identify gods and objects, telling the reader what something is. Whenever a noun phrase is followed by pw and nothing else, translate “it is…” and let the context choose “he”, “she” or “this”.

blocks.html: The third sentence without a verb says what something is like: “he is good”, “his house is beautiful”. It uses an adjective (Adjectives) as the predicate and a dependent pronoun (Dependent Pronouns) or a noun as the subject.

In an adjectival sentence the adjective comes first and the subject follows: nfr sw “he is good”, nfr pr=f “his house is good”. The adjective has no ending here, even with a feminine or plural subject.
