blocks.html: Compare two orders with the same words. pr=f nfr, with the adjective after the noun, is a phrase: “his good house”. nfr pr=f, with the adjective first, is a sentence: “his house is good”. Word order in Egyptian is strict, and it is often the only thing that tells a phrase from a sentence.

The adjective in this sentence does not agree: nfr sj “she is good”, nfr st “they are good”, with nfr unchanged. Adjectival sentences are common in praise of gods and kings and in descriptions: “great is his strength”, “beautiful is her face”.

Why does the adjective come first? Egyptian puts the new information, the predicate, at the head of this kind of sentence, as in English exclamations like “Great is the Lord”. The dependent pronoun, which must follow another word, fits naturally after it.

Reading nfr sw as “a good him”, a noun phrase. An adjective first, then its subject, is a sentence: “he is good”. Check: an adjective that stands before its noun or pronoun is a predicate; an adjective after a noun is a description.

blocks.html: Egyptian numbers are among the easiest things to read in hieroglyphs, because they work by simple addition. You need only seven signs and the idea of sign kinds from Three Kinds of Signs.

Each power of ten has its own sign, repeated as often as needed: the stroke 𓏤 1, the hobble 𓎆 10, the coil of rope 𓍢 100, the lotus 𓆼 1,000, the finger 𓂭 10,000, the tadpole 𓆐 100,000 and the god Heh 𓁨 1,000,000. Add them up.

blocks.html: Write a number by its parts, the largest first in reading order. 1,234 is one lotus (1,000), two coils (200), three hobbles (30) and four strokes (4). Repeated signs are arranged in neat stacks of two to four, so that a number fits the square groups of Groups and Quadrats. There is no sign for zero, and none is needed: if a number has no tens, the hobbles are simply left out.

blocks.html: Big numbers appear in temple inventories, in records of booty and in the offering formula’s “thousand of bread, thousand of beer”. The Heh sign, a kneeling god holding up his arms, also stands for the word ḥḥ “millions”, and so for “eternity”: wishes for “millions of years” are common on royal monuments.

Why is this system easy to read but slow to write? It is additive, like Roman numerals without subtraction: each sign has one value, wherever it stands. Reading means counting signs. But a number like 999 needs 27 signs. Scribes writing accounts in hieratic used quicker forms, with single signs for 2, 3, 20, 30 and so on.

Reading numerals by position, like our digits, so that two coils followed by three strokes become “23”. Egyptian numerals simply add up: two coils are 200, three strokes 3, total 203. Check: multiply each kind of sign by its value and add.

blocks.html: Counting things combines the numerals of Numerals with the nouns and plurals of The Plural. The main rule is about order, and it is the opposite of English.
In writing, the number follows the noun it counts: zꜣ 3 “three sons”, pr 10 “ten houses”. Ordinals (“second, third”) add -nw to the number: snnw “second”, ḫmtnw “third”; “first” is tpj.

blocks.html: Egyptologists usually transliterate the numeral as a figure: kꜣ 5 “five bulls”, rmṯ 40 “forty people”. Spelling of the noun varies: in lists and accounts it is often written without a plural ending or plural strokes, as if the number were enough. The number words themselves (wꜥ “one”, sn “two”, ḫmt “three”…) are rarely spelled out, because the numeral signs were quicker.

blocks.html: From two to nine the ordinal adds -nw to the number; from ten on, Egyptian uses mḥ “filling” before the number, so mḥ 20 is “the twentieth”, the one that fills twenty. “First” is the nisbe tpj from tp “head” (see Nisbe Adjectives).

Why does the number follow? In Egyptian the head of a noun phrase comes first and everything that describes it follows: adjectives, demonstratives, possessors and numbers alike. “Sons, three” follows the same pattern as “son, good” and “son, this”.
Putting the number before the noun, as in English “three sons”. In writing, the number follows: zꜣ 3. Check: in an inscription, read the noun, then look right after it for the numeral signs.

Numbers also follow the noun in measures and prices. A text may list t 100 “100 loaves” or give a field’s size as a number after the word for the measure. When you read an account, take each noun with the number that comes right after it, and you will rarely go wrong.

blocks.html: Egyptian documents are dated, often very precisely. But a date does not give a year counted from one fixed point, as ours do. It counts from the start of the reigning king’s rule. You need the numerals and ordinals of Counting Things.
A date gives the regnal year, the month of a season and the day: ḥꜣt-zp 5 ꜣbd 2 ꜣḫt sw 10 “year 5, second month of Akhet (the Flood), day 10”. Egyptologists write it “Year 5, II Akhet 10”.

blocks.html: The civil calendar had three seasons of four months each: ꜣḫt Akhet, the Flood; prt Peret, the Emergence or Growing season; and šmw Shemu, the Harvest or Low Water. Every month had 30 days, and five extra days were added at the end of the year, making 365. There was no leap day, so the civil calendar slowly drifted against the real seasons, by about one day every four years.

blocks.html: The day sign in dates is the sun 𓇳, read sw here (it reads rꜥ and hrw elsewhere). The year group was once read rnpt-zp; today ḥꜣt-zp is the usual reading. The word zp “occasion” goes back to the Old Kingdom, when years were named after the count of cattle held every year or two.

Why count years by reigns? Because the king was the center of the order of the world, and each reign was a new beginning. To turn such dates into years BC, historians need the length of every reign and the order of the kings, which is why king lists and chronology matter so much (and why early dates are given with “c.”).

Expecting a year counted from one fixed point. “Year 5” means the fifth year of the king named in the text, or the king then reigning. Check: a date is only fully useful when you know which king it belongs to.

blocks.html: The most common words on Egyptian monuments are royal names. A king did not have one name but five, together called the titulary. Each name was a short statement about him, often mentioning a god, so you will need honorific transposition from Honorific Transposition.
The five royal names, in order: the Horus name, the Two Ladies name, the Golden Horus name, the throne name (in a cartouche, after nsw-bjt) and the birth name (in a cartouche, after zꜣ-rꜥ).

blocks.html: The Horus name is the oldest: the first kings of Egypt are known almost only by it. The full set of five was standard by the Middle Kingdom. The throne name was taken at the coronation; the birth name was the name the king had as a prince. Kings who shared a birth name, like the several Amenhoteps or Ramesses, are told apart by their throne names; modern books number them instead (Amenhotep III, Ramesses II).

blocks.html: Why five names? Each one tied the king to a different part of Egyptian kingship: Horus, the god whose living image he was; the two goddesses of Upper and Lower Egypt; gold, the eternal metal of the gods; the double kingship of the Two Lands; and Ra, whose son he was. Taken together the names made a short statement of what the king was meant to be.

Thinking that “Ramesses” was the king’s only name. It is his birth name. His throne name was Usermaatre Setepenre, and in his own time that was the name most often used for him, by foreigners too. Check: when a cartouche follows nsw-bjt, it holds the throne name, not the familiar modern name.

blocks.html: The two most important royal names, the throne name and the birth name from The Five Royal Names, are written inside an oval ring, the cartouche. Two titles stand in front of the cartouches, and learning to separate titles from names is the key to reading them.
The throne name follows nsw-bjt “King of Upper and Lower Egypt”; the birth name follows zꜣ-rꜥ “son of Ra”. The titles stand outside, before the cartouche; the name is inside.

blocks.html: nsw-bjt is written with the sedge plant 𓇓, the plant of Upper Egypt, and the bee 𓆤, the insect of Lower Egypt. Literally it means “he of the sedge and the bee”. zꜣ-rꜥ is the pintail duck 𓅭 zꜣ “son” and the sun 𓇳 rꜥ “Ra”: the king as the son of the sun god.

The oval is a stretched form of the šnw ring, a loop of rope tied at one end, perhaps a symbol of everything the sun encircles. Egyptians called it šnw; the modern word “cartouche” comes from French soldiers of Napoleon’s expedition, who thought it looked like a cartridge. The knot is at the end of the name, so it also shows the direction of reading.

blocks.html: Kings’ names are often followed by short wishes, such as ꜥnḫ ḏt “may he live forever” or dj ꜥnḫ “given life”. These too stand outside the cartouche. Queens and princesses were sometimes given cartouches as well.

Why keep titles outside the ring? The cartouche protects and marks the name itself, the part that was the king’s own. The titles describe his office and stay the same from king to king: every king was nsw-bjt and zꜣ-rꜥ. Separating them made it easy to see whose monument it was.
Reading nsw-bjt as part of the name. It is a title placed before the cartouche, shared by every king. Check: only what is inside the ring is the name.

Read a cartouche sign by sign, then check for a god’s name written first. In twt-ꜥnḫ-jmn Tutankhamun, Amun’s name is written first but read last; in jmn-ḥtp Amenhotep it is read first, because it belongs first.

blocks.html: Why is the god sometimes read last? Many royal names are short sentences or phrases about a god: “living image of Amun”, “enduring is the form of Ra”. Grammar puts the god at the end (“image of Amun”), but honor puts him at the front of the writing. When the god is the subject of the sentence (“Amun is content”), he comes first in both.

Reading the god’s name first because it is written first: “Amun-tut-ankh”. Translate the name: if the god is the possessor or comes after a verb or adjective in the meaning, he is read last. Check with a known name: Tutankhamun, not Amuntutankh.

blocks.html: Thousands of stelae, false doors and coffins begin with the same words: ḥtp-dj-nsw. This is the offering formula, the prayer that provided the dead with food and drink forever. It uses honorific transposition (Honorific Transposition) and the indirect genitive (The Indirect Genitive).
The formula begins ḥtp-dj-nsw “an offering that the king gives”, names a god, usually Osiris or Anubis, with his epithets, lists the gifts, and ends n kꜣ n N “for the ka of N”, the dead person.

blocks.html: The idea behind the formula is a chain of giving. The king, as the one who made offerings to all the gods, gives an offering to a god of the dead; the god in turn provides for the deceased. In practice the family or a priest made the offerings at the tomb, but the formula placed them under the king’s name and the god’s care, and its words were thought to make the offerings real for the dead even when no food was brought.

The gods most often named are Osiris, wsjr nb ḏdw nṯr ꜥꜣ nb ꜣbḏw “Osiris, lord of Busiris, the great god, lord of Abydos”, and Anubis, jnpw tpj ḏw=f “Anubis who is upon his mountain” or nb tꜣ ḏsr “lord of the sacred land”, the necropolis.

Grammarians translate the opening in slightly different ways: Gardiner wrote “a boon which the king gives”; others prefer “an offering given by the king”. The structure of the phrase has been studied closely and is still discussed, but the meaning is not in doubt.

Why is it so common? A tomb or stela was meant to keep its owner alive in memory and to supply him or her for eternity. The formula did both: it named the dead person and, read aloud by any passer-by, it brought the offerings into being. Many stelae ask visitors directly to say it.

Translating ḥtp-dj-nsw word for word in written order: “king, offering, gives”. The king is written first but read last: “an offering that the king gives”. Check: the god named next receives the offering; the king gives it.

The formula continues prt-ḫrw “an invocation offering”, literally “a going forth of the voice”, of t ḥnqt “bread and beer”, kꜣw ꜣpdw “oxen and fowl”, šs mnḫt “alabaster and linen” and ḫt nbt nfrt wꜥbt “every good and pure thing”.

blocks.html: prt means “going forth” and ḫrw “voice”. A prt-ḫrw is the offering that comes forth when the words are spoken. Many stelae address the living: “O you who live on earth, who pass by this stela… say: a thousand of bread and beer for the ka of N”. Speaking the formula was itself an offering.

Why these gifts? They are the necessities and comforts of an Egyptian household: bread and beer for daily food, meat and fowl for feasts, linen for clothing, and stone vessels for oils and perfumes. The dead were expected to need them as the living did, so the formula promised them for eternity.

Reading prt-ḫrw as just “voice”. It is the offering that comes forth at the call of the voice, an invocation offering. Check: ḫrw alone is “voice”; with prt it names a kind of offering, followed by the list of what is offered.

blocks.html: A stela names its owner with titles before the name and epithets after it. Reading them tells you who the person was: a scribe, a priest, an overseer of works, a lady of the house. This lesson builds on The Offering Formula, since titles fill the end of the formula.
Titles come before the name: sš “scribe”, jmj-rꜣ “overseer”, ḥm-nṯr “priest”. Epithets come after it: mꜣꜥ-ḫrw “true of voice”, said of the blessed dead.

blocks.html: mꜣꜥ-ḫrw “true of voice” (often translated “justified”) follows the names of the dead, rather like “the late” or “of blessed memory”. It expresses the idea of being vindicated, found truthful, as in the judgment of the dead. Another common epithet is jmꜣḫw “revered one”, often with ḫr and a god: “revered before Osiris”. Neither is part of the name.

Women’s titles appear too. The Middle Kingdom often calls a married woman nbt pr “lady of the house”, and women could also hold priestly titles in the service of goddesses. A family stela may list a whole household, each person with titles and epithets.

Why so many titles? Titles were how Egyptian society placed people: by office, rank and service to king and gods. On a funerary monument, a full list of titles recorded a life’s achievement and assured the owner’s status in the next world.

Taking mꜣꜥ-ḫrw as part of the name. It is an epithet for the blessed dead. Check: titles come before the name, epithets after; the name is usually the word or words between them, often with a seated man or woman determinative.

blocks.a: title sš, name Nakht, epithet mꜣꜥ-ḫrw

blocks.html: Titles can be stacked: an official may list ten or more, from honorary ranks at court to his practical job. Read them one by one; each usually ends where the next title word begins. A name follows the last title, and the epithets close the sequence.
